author: Carlos Martinez
title: Indianapolis Motor Speedway Oval: Trim, Drafting, and Speed
description: Master Indy's high-speed oval with proper trim setup and drafting technique. Real lap data and MOZA R9 feedback insights for consistent top-10 pace.

sections.p: Indianapolis Motor Speedway's 2.5-mile D-shaped oval is a masterclass in precision, aero sensitivity, and drafting strategy. I've spent enough laps here on my MOZA R9 to understand why Indy humbles drivers who treat it like a road course—the track demands a different skill set entirely. Trim, downforce balance, and how you position yourself relative to traffic dictate your pace far more than raw throttle control.

This guide walks you through the fundamentals of oval setup and race craft specific to Indy's unique shape. Whether you're chasing your first top-10 or grinding toward a license upgrade, understanding how trim and drafting interact will compress your learning curve by weeks.

sections.h2: What Trim Actually Does at Indy

sections.p: Trim is your front wing angle. Higher trim (more angle) adds downforce and stability but kills top speed on the straights. Lower trim gives you speed but makes the car loose, especially in Turns 1 and 3. Indy is a straight-line speed track, so the trim sweet spot is shallower than most road courses—typically between -2.0 and -4.0 degrees depending on your car class.

On my R9, I can feel the difference immediately. At Indy's speed—we're talking 220+ mph on the straights in an Indycar—even a half-degree of trim change shifts your brake marker by two or three feet and your exit speed by 2–3 mph. That sounds small until you're trying to get a tow and hold line into Turn 1 with a car one position ahead.

list: Higher trim (more downforce): Stable through turns, earlier brake point, lower top speed on straights
Lower trim (less downforce): Faster on straights, looser entry, harder to manage traffic
Sweet spot for most classes: -2.5 to -3.5 degrees, adjusted for your baseline setup and fuel load

sections.tip: Trim is your first tuning lever. Before you fiddle with springs or bars, get trim right. A half-degree change costs or gains ~1 mph on the straightaway and 0.05 seconds per lap. Your brake balance matters less here than it does on road courses.

sections.p: Drafting at Indy isn't just about slipstreaming—it's a high-stakes positioning game. A good tow can be worth 3–5 mph on the straight. A bad line through the draft can cost you an overtake or lock you into a poor exit that ruins your next lap.

The two straights at Indy are where you gain or lose time. The backmarker straight (the long one) is where you'll set up passes. The front straight is shorter but tighter to the pit entrance, so traffic management there feels claustrophobic in a full field. On the oval portions (Turns 1–2 and 3–4), there's minimal draft benefit—you're fighting aero and momentum.

When you're behind someone, you sit roughly one car length (~50 feet) back on the straight. Too far back and the tow is worthless. Too close and you'll damage your front wing on their rear wing or run into them under braking. The MOZA R9's FFB is sensitive enough that I can feel the suction pull me forward when I'm in the sweet spot—that's your cue.

list: Stay within one car length on the straight to get effective draft benefit
Back off slightly into the turn—aero wash can destabilize your entry
Exit the turn alone if possible, then hunt the next tow into the next straight
Watch your mirror into the turns; a car behind you will dive low if you're loose

sections.p: The actual pass happens in the turn or exit. You catch a tow down the straight, then use your superior exit speed (from fresh tires or setup) to get a run into the turn. As you brake, you start to move down toward the pass lane. The car ahead will either lift or block. If they block, you either back off or go three-wide—three-wide at Indy usually ends badly.

I've found that on the MOZA R9, the FFB feedback through the brake and into the turn tells me a lot about my stability relative to the car ahead. If the road feel is choppy or pulling me offline, I'm likely fighting aero wash and should abort. If the wheel feels planted, I've found clean air and can commit to the pass.

sections.h2: Brake Balance, Turn-In, and Sustained Speed

sections.p: Indy's turns are long and flat. You're not trail-braking hard; you're trail-braking *gently*. The goal is to preserve momentum and exit speed because the straights are where the race is won. Brake bias sits around 53–55% front on most setups, and you want to avoid locking the rears on downshifts into the turns.

list: Brake deep but smooth; locking the rear at Indy means a spin or at best a slow-speed exit
Downshift early to avoid engine braking surprises mid-corner
Apex speed is less important than exit speed; run a high line through the turn if it helps you get power down earlier
Let the car roll through the middle and focus on a strong exit onto the straight

sections.h2: Setup Baseline for Different Car Classes

sections.p: Indycars are the bread-and-butter oval car. Trim typically runs -2.5 to -3.0 degrees depending on downforce level (low, medium, high). Fuel load makes a huge difference—a light car (low fuel for qualifying) needs more downforce and slightly higher brake bias. A full tank (race fuel) gets slightly lower trim and softer front springs to manage weight transfer.

list: Low downforce qualifying: trim -2.0, brake bias 54%, soft front bar for stability
Medium downforce race: trim -3.0, brake bias 53%, balanced setup for tire management
High downforce (traffic): trim -3.5, brake bias 52%, prioritize stability in pack

sections.p: Stock cars run higher downforce by nature. Trim sits around -3.5 to -4.5 degrees. The bigger, heavier car means more brake bias (typically 54–56%) and stiffer springs to handle the load. Drafting is even more critical for stock cars than Indycars because a stock car alone is slow. In a pack, you'll run 2–3 mph faster than a lone car.

Indy is a low-downforce, high-speed oval, which means tires don't overheat easily and tend to last a long time. Your strategy revolves around fuel windows and track position, not tire survival. A typical race strategy is: pit early if you're behind, pit late if you're ahead, and manage fuel mileage carefully.

Tire wear is even and predictable—no sudden drops. You'll see maybe a 0.3–0.5 second-per-lap spread from lap 1 to lap 50 on a fresh set, then it levels off. That means if you're running low downforce and expecting tires to build grip, you'll be disappointed. The track and setup matter far more than tire cycle.

sections.tip: Indy races are won on fuel strategy and pit stops, not tire saves. Run your pace, trust your setup, and nail your fuel calculations. A miscalculation that costs you one pit stop costs you the race.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them

list: Running trim too high: You feel stable but lose 3+ mph on the straights and miss draft opportunities. Lower it 0.5–1.0 degree and re-brake earlier into turns.

Brake locking into turns: Indy punishes locking the rears with a spin. Ease off the pedal slightly earlier and focus on modulation through the turn. Load-cell pedals like my MOZA CRP2 make this much easier to feel.
Ignoring fuel: Running out of fuel two laps early or coasting fuel all race is a morale killer. Calculate your fuel mileage during warmup and stick to it.
Following too close: You're fighting aero wash instead of benefiting from it. Back off to one car length and feel the tow pull you forward.
Not adjusting trim for fuel load: A light car (qualifying) needs less trim than a race car. Adjust -0.5 to -1.0 degree as fuel weight changes.

sections.p: When I review telemetry on a fast lap, I'm looking for three things: consistent brake release points (showing confidence and repeatability), smooth throttle application (no spikes or erratic inputs), and top speed aligned with my trim setting. If my top speed is 8+ mph lower than expected, trim is too high or I'm running too much wing. If I'm locking rears into turns, my brake bias is too rear-biased or I'm trail-braking too aggressively.

list: Compare brake marker distances lap-to-lap; variance means inconsistent inputs or confidence issues
Check top speed on each straight; loss of speed mid-race suggests tire wear or fuel weight, not setup failure
Review gear selections; wrong downshift points waste time and risk engine braking issues
Plot apex speeds and exit speeds side-by-side; higher apex speed with lower exit is a sign you need better momentum management

faqs.q: What trim setting should I start with at Indy?
faqs.a: Start at -3.0 degrees for your car class. If you're losing speed on the straights or your draft feels ineffective, drop to -2.5. If you're too loose entering the turns or spinning out, raise to -3.5. Adjust in 0.5-degree steps and take 3-4 full laps to feel the change. Remember trim affects top speed, entry stability, and draft quality simultaneously.

faqs.q: How close should I follow another car to get the tow?
faqs.a: Stay within one car length, roughly 40-60 feet depending on your speed. Too far back and the slipstream doesn't help your speed. Too close and you're in the dirty air behind their wing, which destabilizes your car and you'll run into them under braking. The sweet spot is when you feel a slight tug forward in your steering wheel feedback—that's clean air being pushed behind them toward you.

faqs.q: Should I use a lower brake bias at Indy than a road course?
faqs.a: Not necessarily lower, but often slightly higher. Indy's long, flat turns mean you're not carrying speed mid-corner, so rear locking is less of a concern than on road courses. Typical brake bias at Indy runs 52-55% front depending on setup and fuel load. The key is smooth modulation—your pressure curve matters more than the bias number. Locking the rear is catastrophic at Indy because you have nowhere to go but the wall.

faqs.q: How do I know if my trim is optimized for the fuel load I'm carrying?
faqs.a: Run two practice laps at the same fuel level, then pit, add fuel, and run two more. If your top speed on the straights drops by more than 2-3 mph and your brake markers are inconsistent, your trim is out of sync with the weight. Lower trim by 0.5 degree to compensate for the extra weight, then re-test. A well-balanced setup feels planted and repeatable regardless of fuel load, though you may lose 0.2-0.3 seconds per lap from weight alone.
